title: The Do Now Dilemma: Fixing the Ragged Start
author: Dr. Emily Manuel
summary: Manuel tackles a microscopic but critical lesson design problem: the ragged start that occurs when students arrive at different times. While education best practice dictates a Do Now should already be on the board for students to start immediately upon entry, real classrooms see students trickling in over minutes. This creates a dilemma: move on and lose the latecomers, wait and lose momentum for punctual students. Manuel's solution is a specific entry routine that synchronizes nearly the entire class to start at the same time, regardless of arrival, ensuring consistent pace and settlement. She demonstrates how classroom management at the door level directly impacts lesson flow and student focus.
points: The ragged start is a microscopic but pervasive problem: students arriving at different times means some finish the Do Now before others have started, creating uneven lesson pace and behavior management challenges.
If you move on to review the Do Now immediately, you lose latecomers; if you wait, you lose momentum and bore early arrivals who finish in minutes.

Trying to resolve ragged starts by having early finishers do extension tasks often backfires, creating an unsettled room and giving latecomers, often those with behavioral needs, a disruptive entrance.

An intentional entry routine that synchronizes student settlement can solve this: ensuring nearly all students start at the same time, finish at roughly the same time, and maintain focus regardless of arrival time.
The routines work because they control the rhythm of entry and mental engagement, not because they demand perfection, making lessons more manageable and focused from the first minute.
quotes: When students walk into your classroom, the Do Now should already be on the board. It's standard practice, championed by experts like Craig Barton.
This creates a Ragged Start. Student A arrives perfectly on time, sits down, and cracks on. Student B arrives 3 minutes later. Student C strolls in 4 minutes late.
By the time the first 5 minutes are up, Student A has finished and is waiting, bored. Student C hasn't even written the date yet.
If you move on to marking the do now, you lose the latecomers. If you wait for the latecomers, you lose the momentum of the punctual students and the high attainers who finish early.

I realised that by staying at the door greeting students individually as they trickled in, I was inadvertently allowing the energy of the room to leak out.” Archived from dremanuele.substack.com on April 20, 2026 by Tim.
